snip.t: Naloxone is for opioids, flumazenil for benzodiazepines, atropine for organophosphates and vitamin K for warfarin.
Most psychotropic drugs work at this point: they block reuptake (SSRIs), block receptors (antipsychotics), block breakdown (MAO inhibitors) or enhance receptor action (benzodiazepines).
Agitation and insomnia: short-term benzodiazepine (lorazepam or diazepam).
Emergency rapid tranquillisation: haloperidol IM (with an anticholinergic) or lorazepam; avoid IM olanzapine together with a parenteral benzodiazepine (respiratory and cardiac depression).

qs.q: A patient with anxiety is prescribed a benzodiazepine. They report feeling relaxed but also confused. Which mechanism best explains the confusion?
o: The medication raises dopamine levels, potentially causing hallucinations and mental confusion.
The medication blocks serotonin transmission, possibly altering perception and leading to confusion.
The medication boosts GABA activity, which may impair cognition and produce confusion.
The medication reduces norepinephrine reuptake, possibly causing agitation and confusion.
The medication increases acetylcholine activity, which might result in memory loss and confusion.
qs.e: Benzodiazepines enhance GABA activity, which can lead to cognitive impairment and confusion.
qs.s: Weekly Year 1: Behavioural Sciences Exam - October 30, 2026 (Section A: MCQs)

qs.q: A medical student is asked to differentiate the pharmacological action of benzodiazepines from barbiturates on the GABA-A receptor channel. Which statement correctly distinguishes benzodiazepines?
o: They increase the duration of chloride channel opening
They activate the channel directly without requiring GABA
They increase the frequency of chloride channel opening
They bind exclusively to the outer membrane lipid layer
They block chloride influx to depolarize the membrane
qs.e: Benzodiazepines increase channel opening frequency, whereas barbiturates prolong the duration of channel openings.
qs.s: Weekly Pharmacology Exam - October 30, 2026 (Section A: MCQs)

qs.q: An anxious patient is given a benzodiazepine for acute symptom relief. At the molecular level, how do benzodiazepines exert their therapeutic effect on the central nervous system?
o: Increasing the frequency of chloride channel opening at GABA-A
Inhibiting the breakdown of acetylcholine in synaptic clefts
Acting as direct full agonists at the glutamate receptor
Competitively blocking postsynaptic dopamine receptor subtypes
qs.e: Benzodiazepines enhance GABA-A receptor activity by increasing the frequency of chloride channel opening, which produces an inhibitory central nervous system effect. They do not act on glutamate receptors or acetylcholinesterase.
qs.s: Master Pharmacokinetics, Dynamics & Antimicrobial Drugs: MCQs

qs.q: A patient with status epilepticus continues to seize despite adequate doses of a benzodiazepine and a second-line agent. This condition is best described as:
o: New-onset refractory status
Febrile status epilepticus
Refractory status epilepticus
Superrefractory status epilepticus
qs.e: Refractory status epilepticus is defined as SE that fails to respond to at least two medications, such as a benzodiazepine and another agent. Superrefractory SE requires failure to resolve or recurrence within 24 hours despite continuous infusion therapy.
qs.s: Acute management of seizure and status epilepticus: MCQs

qs.q: A child with status epilepticus has failed to respond to a benzodiazepine and is now receiving urgent therapy. What is the recommended loading dose of fosphenytoin?
o: Loading dose of 20-40 mg/kg
Loading dose of 20 PE/kg
Loading dose of 30-60 mg/kg
Loading dose of 10 PE/kg
qs.e: The note specifies that fosphenytoin is given at a loading dose of 20 PE/kg. The ranges 20-40 mg/kg and 30-60 mg/kg correspond to valproate and levetiracetam, respectively.
qs.s: Acute management of seizure and status epilepticus: MCQs

qs.q: What is the primary mechanism contributing to the decreased effectiveness of benzodiazepines as status epilepticus duration increases?
o: Failure of desensitization of AMPA receptors
Development of drug resistance via metabolism
Reduction of GABA inhibition via internalization
Increased cerebral metabolic rate over blood flow
qs.e: The note states that GABA-mediated inhibition is reduced due to intracellular internalization of GABAA receptors, explaining why benzodiazepines become less effective. AMPA receptor failure contributes to sustained excitability but is not the direct mechanism for benzodiazepine failure.
qs.s: Acute management of seizure and status epilepticus: MCQs

qs.q: If seizures persist 5 minutes after the initial benzodiazepine dose, what is the recommended next step in management?
o: Administer a second dose of benzodiazepine
Administer intravenous phenobarbital
Start continuous infusion of midazolam
Perform an emergency head CT scan
qs.e: The note states that if seizures persist 5 minutes after the initial dose, a second dose of the benzodiazepine should be given. Urgent therapy with other agents is reserved for failure after the second dose.
qs.s: Acute management of seizure and status epilepticus: MCQs

qs.q: Which of the following is a potential side effect of all first-line benzodiazepine options for status epilepticus?
o: Potential risk of severe neutropenia
Potential risk of hepatic dysfunction
Potential risk of metabolic acidosis
Potential risk of respiratory depression
qs.e: The note explicitly states that respiratory depression is a potential side effect for all first-line benzodiazepine options, requiring monitoring. Hepatic dysfunction is a contraindication for valproate, not a side effect of benzodiazepines.
qs.s: Acute management of seizure and status epilepticus: MCQs
